title: Secure Defaults & Fail-Safe Design
summary: Designing APIs and configuration so the safest option is also the default one, and deciding deliberately what a failed security check should do.

slides.markdown:
Most developers using a library, framework, or API never read every configuration option — they take the default and move on. That single observation is the entire argument for **secure by default**: whatever the default behavior is, that's the behavior most of your users will actually ship, whether or not it was the safe choice.

This topic covers two closely related ideas: designing defaults so the safe path requires the least effort, and — a decision that trips up even experienced engineers — deciding explicitly what should happen when a security check itself fails to run at all, which is a subtly different question from what happens when a check runs and says no.

slides.subTitle: The safest option should require the least effort
slides.markdown:
The design principle: whatever a user of your API, library, or configuration does with the least effort — leaving a setting untouched, calling a function with no extra arguments — should be the **safest** available behavior, not the most permissive or convenient one.

A storage bucket that's private unless someone explicitly makes it public is secure by default; a bucket that's public unless someone explicitly locks it down is not, even if locking it down is just as easy — because most people won't do either step deliberately, they'll just accept whatever came out of the box. A web framework that escapes HTML by default in its templating engine, requiring an explicit `|safe`-style opt-out to render raw HTML, is secure by default; one that renders raw HTML unless you remember to escape it is not.

The underlying insight: **effort predicts behavior far better than intent.** Assuming developers will "just remember" to configure the safe option is a bet against how software actually gets built under real deadlines, and secure-by-default design is the way to stop needing developers to remember at all.

slides.subTitle: What should happen when a check itself errors
slides.markdown:
| | Fail-safe (fail-closed) | Fail-open |
|---|---|---|
| Behavior when a check errors | Deny/reject — treat an inability to evaluate as a "no" | Allow/proceed — treat an inability to evaluate as a "yes" |
| Failure mode it causes | Availability impact — legitimate requests blocked while the check is broken | Security impact — requests bypass the check entirely while it's broken |
| Where it's usually the right default | Authorization, authentication, payment processing — anywhere an incorrect "allow" is the worse outcome | Rarely the right default for security-relevant checks; sometimes acceptable for non-security features |
| The trap | None if applied deliberately | Often introduced accidentally, by code that never anticipated the check itself could error |

This is a genuinely different question from "what happens when the check runs and says no" — that's ordinary access control, and denying is obviously correct. Fail-safe vs fail-open is about the case where the check **can't run at all** — a downstream permission service is down, a database lookup times out, an exception is thrown mid-evaluation — and for almost any security-relevant check, the correct default is to treat that as a denial, not a free pass.

slides.sectionTitle: Opt-out security features are a smell
slides.subTitle: Security should be opt-in to disable
slides.markdown:
A useful design litmus test: is a given security feature **on by default, with an explicit opt-out** for the rare case that needs it disabled, or **off by default, with an explicit opt-in** to turn it on? The second pattern is a smell, because it means every consumer who doesn't know to opt in — which, per the earlier slide, is most of them — ships without the protection.

Concrete examples of the healthy pattern: a web framework that CSRF-protects every form by default, requiring an explicit annotation to exempt a specific endpoint that genuinely doesn't need it (an unauthenticated public API, say). A database ORM that parameterizes queries by default, requiring deliberate, explicit raw-SQL usage to bypass it. In both cases, the protection is the path of least resistance, and *skipping* it is the part that takes deliberate, visible effort — which also means a code reviewer has something concrete to notice and question.

slides.sectionTitle: Why "batteries-included" defaults remove whole vulnerability classes
slides.markdown:
The strongest version of secure-by-default doesn't just make the safe option easy — it makes the *unsafe* option structurally unavailable or clearly abnormal-looking. A modern web framework that auto-escapes all template output doesn't just default to safety; it removes the entire class of "forgot to escape user input" XSS bugs from every template written using its standard mechanism, for every developer who ever uses it, without any of them needing to think about XSS at all.

This is a genuinely different scale of impact than "remember to call the escaping function" — that approach still requires every individual call site to get it right, forever, while a framework-level default gets it right everywhere at once, retroactively, the moment the framework itself is correct. It's the same structural-enforcement idea that recurs across this whole area (admission controllers in Kubernetes, least-privilege IAM as a policy gate) applied at the framework-design level instead of the deployment level: fix the vulnerability class once, upstream, rather than asking every downstream user to individually avoid it.

slides.sectionTitle: Choosing fail-open deliberately, where it's actually appropriate
slides.markdown:
Fail-safe isn't universally correct for every kind of check — the principle applies specifically to **security-relevant** decisions, and treating every possible check as security-relevant leads to over-applying fail-safe in places where it just causes unnecessary outages for no security benefit.

A non-security feature flag check that fails — say, a recommendation-personalization service being down — reasonably fails open to a default, generic experience rather than blocking the whole page; there's no security property being protected there, only a nice-to-have. Similarly, some rate-limiting implementations deliberately fail open under infrastructure failure (treating an inability to check the current rate as "don't block") because the alternative — a rate limiter's own outage taking down the entire service it's supposed to be protecting — is judged worse than temporarily allowing traffic through unthrottled.

The actual skill being tested isn't "always choose fail-safe" — it's correctly classifying which checks are security-relevant (authentication, authorization, payment validation — fail-safe) versus which are availability/UX trade-offs where fail-open is a defensible, deliberate choice, and being able to articulate which category a given check falls into and why.

slides.sectionTitle: Auditing a codebase for accidental fail-open
slides.subTitle: The senior-level nuance
slides.markdown:
Accidental fail-open is rarely a deliberate design decision — it's usually a bare `try/except` (or `try/catch`) wrapped around a permission check by someone thinking only about crash prevention, not about what the code does when the exception fires. The check throws, the exception is caught to stop the request from 500-ing, and whatever code runs after the catch block proceeds as if the check had passed, because nobody explicitly wrote the deny path for the error case.

A senior-level audit habit: for every security-relevant check in a codebase, explicitly trace what happens on **every** exit path — not just "check passes" and "check fails," but "check throws," "check times out," "check's dependency is unreachable." A surprising number of real authorization bugs are found exactly this way: not by breaking the logic that says yes or no, but by finding the path where the logic never got a chance to say anything at all, and the surrounding code silently treated that as permission granted.

slides.sectionTitle: Numbers: the reach of a single framework default
slides.markdown:
A popular web framework can be running behind hundreds of thousands or millions of applications simultaneously. Changing one default in that framework — auto-escaping template output, parameterizing queries, CSRF protection on by default — propagates the fix to every one of those applications the next time they update the dependency, with zero code changes required in the applications themselves.

Compare that to the alternative of publishing a security advisory saying "remember to escape your template output": that advisory reaches some fraction of the framework's users, some fraction of those actually act on it, and the ones who joined the ecosystem after the advisory was published may never see it at all. The leverage of a secure default versus a best-practice recommendation isn't a small difference — it's closer to "fixes for every user automatically" versus "fixes for whoever happens to read and apply it," which is why framework and library maintainers treat default-behavior changes as one of their highest-leverage security levers.
